intended_object: The canonical simultaneous range–kernel decomposition for two commuting idempotent endomorphisms p, q of an R-module M: M ≅ (im p ∩ im q) × (im p ∩ ker q) × (ker p ∩ im q) × (ker p ∩ ker q). The forward map sends x to (pqx, p(1−q)x, (1−p)qx, (1−p)(1−q)x) and the inverse adds the four components. This comes from the docstring and the module documentation.
explanation:
The definition composes the library's general finite-family decomposition `commutingIdempotentsPiEquiv ![p, q]` with a reindexing. The general decomposition is M ≃ Π_{ε : Fin 2 → Bool} jointBlock, built from the complete orthogonal idempotents ∏ (p_i or 1 − p_i). The reindexing turns the four Boolean choices into the four displayed intersection submodules, using `jointBlock_pair` to identify each block with (range or ker of p) ⊓ (range or ker of q). The inverse it writes out sends z to the four inclusions, which is the inverse of that reindexing. The coordinates come in the order the docstring gives: range-range, range-kernel, kernel-range, kernel-kernel.

The hypotheses are the natural ones: a semiring of scalars, with M an additive commutative group because 1 − p has to make sense. Over a mere monoid, M = range p ⊕ ker p can fail. Idempotence and commutation are exactly what the decomposition needs.

It specializes the library's own n-fold version. Even so, it is a specific, standard construction (the two-idempotent case) and not a narrowing of a broader notion that Mathlib provides. My survey of Mathlib's `LinearAlgebra/Projection` and its idempotent and orthogonal-idempotent material turned up only the two-piece complement decomposition (`Submodule.prodEquivOfIsCompl`), not this four-piece one. I did not run a full set of name greps over Mathlib, so the "no counterpart" answer is based on that survey.
